Problem 464. Funding a shared public project: case 4
Knowledge context.
Public goods can benefit many people at once, which creates coordination problems about contributions.
Given facts.

A community project is built only if total voluntary contributions reach 12 tokens. Contributions from 6 households are [4, 1, 2, 3, 4, 1]. Everyone can use the project if it is built, including households that contribute zero.
Rules.
Add contributions and compare with the threshold. A public-good threshold concerns whether the project is produced; it does not by itself decide whether every contribution pattern is fair.
Task.
Is the project built? How many additional tokens, if any, are needed?
Step-by-step solution.
1. Total contribution=4+1+2+3+4+1=15. 2. Compare 15 with threshold 12. 3. Additional amount needed=max(0,12−15)=0.
Answer.
The project is built. Additional tokens needed: 0.
Knowledge takeaway.
Threshold provision and fairness are separate questions; first determine whether enough resources exist.
Formal model.
Sum contributions; compare with provision threshold; compute shortfall.
Problem 465. Funding a shared public project: case 5
Knowledge context.
Public goods can benefit many people at once, which creates coordination problems about contributions.
Given facts.

A community project is built only if total voluntary contributions reach 12 tokens. Contributions from 6 households are [1, 2, 3, 4, 1, 2]. Everyone can use the project if it is built, including households that contribute zero. Cross-domain check: a survey team starts work at 8:00 and works for 2 hour(s) without a break.
Rules.

Add contributions and compare with the threshold. A public-good threshold concerns whether the project is produced; it does not by itself decide whether every contribution pattern is fair. For the cross-domain check, finishing time = starting time + duration.
Task.
Is the project built? How many additional tokens, if any, are needed? Cross-domain check: at what time does the team finish?
Step-by-step solution.
1. Total contribution=1+2+3+4+1+2=13. 2. Compare 13 with threshold 12. 3. Additional amount needed=max(0,12−13)=0. Cross-domain check: 8+2=10, so the team finishes at 10:00.
Answer.
The project is built. Additional tokens needed: 0. Cross-domain answer: 10:00.
Knowledge takeaway.
Threshold provision and fairness are separate questions; first determine whether enough resources exist.
Formal model.
Sum contributions; compare with provision threshold; compute shortfall.
N19. Common resources and avoiding depletion
Problem 466. Using a shared renewable resource: case 1
Knowledge context.
A common resource can be overused when many individually reasonable withdrawals add up to more than regeneration.
Given facts.

A shared fishery has 80 fish at the start of the period and regenerates 10. There are 5 users, each planning to take 3. For this simplified exercise, the stock should not decline below its starting level if use is to be called non-depleting.
Rules.
End stock = start + regeneration − total harvest. Total harvest is number of users × harvest per user.
Task.
What is the end stock? Is the planned use non-depleting under the stated definition? What equal per-user harvest would exactly match regeneration?
Step-by-step solution.
1. Total harvest=5×3=15. 2. End stock=80+10−15=75. 3. To match regeneration exactly, equal harvest per user would be 10÷5=2.00.
Answer.
End stock 75; depleting. Equal regeneration-matching share: 2.00 each.
Knowledge takeaway.
The shared-resource problem appears at the total level, so individual plans must be aggregated.
Formal model.
Commons stock equation plus equal-share benchmark.
